blocks.text: Dataset cleaning is the process of finding and fixing problems in a collected dataset before it gets used for training, malformed entries, inconsistent formatting, missing fields, off-task examples, and mislabeled data.
Skipping or rushing this stage is one of the most common reasons a fine-tuning run underperforms, since a model trained on noisy data tends to learn the noise right alongside the intended pattern.
1. What Cleaning Means for a Fine-Tuning Dataset

blocks.alt: What Cleaning Means for a Fine-Tuning Dataset
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448357274-495066538.png

Cleaning takes the raw, often messy output of the collection stage and turns it into a dataset that reliably represents the task you actually want the model to learn, free of the kinds of errors that would otherwise confuse training.

This stage sits directly after collection and directly before formatting, both covered elsewhere in this module, and the three stages together turn raw examples into a dataset ready for a training run.
2. Removing Corrupted or Malformed Examples
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448357274-585015137.png

Some examples are simply broken, truncated text, garbled characters, or a structure that does not match what the rest of the dataset looks like. These need to be detected and removed before training, since a model cannot learn a meaningful pattern from corrupted input.
Automated checks, verifying that every example has the expected fields and a reasonable length, catch the majority of these problems quickly, without needing to inspect every example by hand.
3. Fixing Encoding and Formatting Inconsistencies
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448357628-185199471.png

Data pulled from different sources often arrives with different character encodings, inconsistent whitespace, or mixed quote styles, small inconsistencies that can quietly degrade training quality if left unaddressed.
Normalizing text early, consistent encoding, consistent whitespace handling, consistent punctuation, removes a source of noise that is easy to fix but easy to overlook.

code.content:
# A simple normalization pass over raw examples
def normalize(example):
    example.text = example.text.strip()
    example.text = example.text.encode("utf-8", "ignore").decode("utf-8")
    example.text = collapse_repeated_whitespace(example.text)
    return example

blocks.text: 4. Handling Missing or Incomplete Fields
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448357630-911583224.png

When an example is missing a required field, sometimes it can be safely filled in or inferred from other available information, and sometimes the example genuinely cannot be salvaged and should be dropped rather than kept with a guessed or empty value.
Keeping an incomplete example with a fabricated value is often worse than dropping it entirely, since the model has no way to tell a filled in placeholder from real signal.
5. Removing Off-Task or Irrelevant Examples
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448357631-356547191.png

Collection processes, especially ones pulling from production logs, often sweep in examples that do not actually match the target task, a conversation that drifted off topic, or a record that technically fits the query but does not represent the behavior you want to teach.
Filtering these out, even at the cost of a smaller final dataset, usually produces a better fine-tuned model than keeping every example regardless of relevance.

blocks.text: 6. Correcting Obvious Labeling Errors
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448357631-898057621.png

Labels, whether a classification tag or a target output, sometimes contain clear mistakes, a support ticket tagged with the wrong category, or a response that does not actually match the instruction it is paired with.
A sample based manual review, checking a random subset of examples by hand, often surfaces labeling error patterns that automated checks alone would miss.

blocks.title: A small sample review catches a lot
blocks.content: Manually reviewing even a few hundred randomly sampled examples frequently surfaces systematic labeling problems that would otherwise go unnoticed until evaluation.

blocks.text: 7. Automated Checks vs Manual Review

Automated checks scale well and catch structural problems quickly, missing fields, malformed text, obviously wrong lengths, but they cannot judge whether an example genuinely represents good task behavior.

Manual review is slower but catches subtler problems, a technically well formed example that is still a poor demonstration of the target behavior, something no automated rule can reliably detect on its own.
8. Cleaning Is Iterative, Not a Single Pass

blocks.alt: Cleaning Is Iterative, Not a Single Pass
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448357632-462481473.png

Cleaning rarely finishes in one pass. A first pass typically catches obvious structural problems, a second pass, often informed by an early training run or evaluation, catches subtler quality issues that only become visible once the model behavior reveals them.
Treating cleaning as a loop that continues alongside evaluation, rather than a box to check once before training starts, tends to produce noticeably better datasets over time.
9. When to Stop Cleaning

Cleaning can, in principle, continue indefinitely, there is always one more edge case to check. A practical stopping point is when a random sample review no longer turns up new categories of problems, and the remaining issues are rare enough not to meaningfully affect training.

At that point, it is usually more productive to move forward to formatting and a first training run, then let evaluation results guide the next round of cleaning, rather than continuing to polish indefinitely.
Worked Example
A team collects five thousand raw customer support tickets for a fine-tuning dataset. An automated pass removes two hundred malformed entries and normalizes encoding across the rest.

A manual review of a three hundred example sample reveals that about five percent of tickets were mislabeled with the wrong category, and a further inspection turns up a batch of off-topic internal test tickets that had leaked into the export. Both issues get fixed, filtered examples get dropped, and the resulting cleaned dataset, though smaller, produces a noticeably better fine-tuned model than the raw export would have.
Common Mistakes

items: Skipping manual review entirely and relying only on automated structural checks
Filling in missing fields with guessed values instead of dropping unsalvageable examples
Treating cleaning as a one time step rather than an iterative process informed by later evaluation
Keeping off-task examples just to preserve dataset size, at the cost of overall quality

blocks.text: Practice

Take a small batch of raw data you have collected or could collect for a task, and manually review twenty examples for the specific problems covered in this topic, malformed entries, missing fields, off-task content, and labeling errors, noting how many of each you actually find.
Key Takeaway

Cleaning turns raw, collected data into a dataset a model can actually learn the right pattern from, and combining fast automated checks with targeted manual review, treated as an iterative process rather than a single pass, is what separates a genuinely clean dataset from one that merely looks clean.
